Complete Study Guide
Exam Release: February 3, 2027
Network

A network is a collection of devices connected together so they can communicate and share resources. It can be as small as two computers connected at home, or as large as millions of servers spread across the globe forming the Internet.
[ Figure: Types of networks: home network, institutional network, regional ISP, global ISP, mobile network — all interconnected ]
Types of networks: home network, institutional network, regional ISP, global ISP, mobile network — all interconnected
The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) Model:-

When two devices from different manufacturers need to communicate — a Cisco router with a Juniper router, a Windows PC with a Linux server — they can do so because everyone follows the same universal rules defined by the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model.

The OSI model divides the complex job of networking into 7 separate layers. Each layer has a specific responsibility and only communicates with the layers directly above and below it. This clean separation means manufacturers can build equipment for one layer without affecting how other layers work.
[ Figure: OSI Model: 7 layers — data flows down the sender's layers (encapsulation), across the wire, then back up the receiver's layers (de-encapsulation) ]
OSI Model: 7 layers — data flows down the sender's layers (encapsulation), across the wire, then back up the receiver's layers (de-encapsulation)

Layer 7 — Application: provides the interfaces and protocols needed by the user's software, enabling applications on different end-systems to communicate. Examples: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), Domain Name System (DNS), File Transfer Protocol (FTP), Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP).

Layer 6 — Presentation: translates data between the application's format and a standard network format. Also handles encryption, decryption, compression, and decompression. Examples: Secure Sockets Layer / Transport Layer Security (SSL/TLS), JPEG, ASCII.
Layer 5 — Session: establishes, maintains, and terminates communication sessions between two applications. Examples: NetBIOS, Remote Procedure Call (RPC).

Layer 4 — Transport: provides end-to-end delivery of data between applications. Handles segmentation, error recovery, and flow control. Adds a header containing source and destination port numbers. Examples: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), User Datagram Protocol (UDP).

Layer 3 — Network: handles logical addressing and routing of packets across different networks through intermediate routers. Adds a header containing source and destination Internet Protocol (IP) addresses. Examples: Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4), IPv6, Open Shortest Path First (OSPF).

Layer 2 — Data Link: handles communication between two directly connected devices on the same local network. Creates frames by adding a header (source and destination Media Access Control (MAC) addresses) and a trailer (Frame Check Sequence (FCS) for error detection). Examples: Ethernet, Wi-Fi (802.11).

Layer 1 — Physical: converts frames into raw bits and transmits them over the physical medium — electrical signals in copper cable, light pulses in fiber optic cable, or electromagnetic waves in wireless.
Encapsulation and Protocol Data Units (PDUs):-

When data is sent, it travels down the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) layers on the sending device, across the physical medium, then back up the layers on the receiving device. As data moves down, each layer adds its own header — and sometimes a trailer. This process is called encapsulation. The data unit at each layer has its own name called a Protocol Data Unit (PDU).
[ Figure: Encapsulation: Application Data → Segment/Datagram (+L4 header) → Packet (+L3 header) → Frame (+L2 header and trailer) → Bits on the wire ]
Encapsulation: Application Data → Segment/Datagram (+L4 header) → Packet (+L3 header) → Frame (+L2 header and trailer) → Bits on the wire

Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP): the Layer 4 Protocol Data Unit (L4PDU). Application data plus a Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) or User Datagram Protocol (UDP) header containing port numbers and transport information.
Packet: the Layer 3 Protocol Data Unit (L3PDU). The segment or datagram plus an Internet Protocol (IP) header containing source and destination IP addresses.
Frame: the Layer 2 Protocol Data Unit (L2PDU). The packet plus an Ethernet header (Media Access Control addresses) and a Frame Check Sequence (FCS) trailer for error detection.
Bits: the Layer 1 Protocol Data Unit (L1PDU). The frame converted into raw electrical, light, or radio signals for physical transmission.
Note: A payload at any layer means everything that layer is carrying, excluding its own header and trailer. For example, the payload of an Ethernet frame (L2PDU) is the IP packet (L3PDU) inside it.
At the receiving device, the process reverses — each layer strips its own header and passes the data upward. This is called de-encapsulation.
Layer 1: The Physical Layer

The Physical Layer is the foundation of all networking. It defines the physical medium that carries raw bits — electrical signals on copper wire, light pulses through fiber optic cable, or radio waves through the air. Every higher layer depends on this layer to physically move data from one place to another.
Transmission Media:-
The physical medium is what carries the actual signal between devices. All transmission media fall into one of two categories:

Wired (guided) media: signals travel through a physical cable that guides the signal from source to destination. Examples: Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP) copper cable, fiber optic cable, coaxial cable.

Wireless (unguided) media: signals travel through the air as electromagnetic waves without any physical conductor. Examples: Wi-Fi local networks, cellular networks (4G/5G), satellite links, terrestrial microwave.
The two main wired media used in modern networks are Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP) copper cable and fiber optic cable. Each is covered in detail below.
Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP) Copper Cables:-

Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP) is the standard copper cable used in wired Ethernet networks. It contains 4 pairs of copper wires — 8 wires total — twisted together inside a plastic outer jacket. Twisting each pair reduces electromagnetic interference (EMI) that would otherwise corrupt the signal.
[ Figure: UTP cable cross-section: 4 color-coded twisted pairs inside an outer plastic jacket, terminating in an RJ-45 connector ]
UTP cable cross-section: 4 color-coded twisted pairs inside an outer plastic jacket, terminating in an RJ-45 connector
The RJ-45 Connector:-

Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP) cables terminate with an RJ-45 connector — the standard plastic plug used for all wired Ethernet connections. It has 8 pins, each corresponding to one of the 8 wires. How those pins are wired at each end determines the cable type.
10BASE-T and 100BASE-T — Pin Usage:-
At speeds of 10 Mbps (10BASE-T) and 100 Mbps (100BASE-TX, also called Fast Ethernet), only 4 of the 8 wires carry data — one pair to transmit and one pair to receive:
Pins 1 & 2: Transmit (TX) from the PC or Router → Receive (RX) on the Switch.
Pins 3 & 6: Receive (RX) on the PC or Router ← Transmit (TX) from the Switch.
[ Figure: 10BASE-T pin diagram: PC pins 1 and 2 (TX) connect to Switch pins 1 and 2 (RX). PC pins 3 and 6 (RX) connect to Switch pins 3 and 6 (TX). ]
10BASE-T pin diagram: PC pins 1 and 2 (TX) connect to Switch pins 1 and 2 (RX). PC pins 3 and 6 (RX) connect to Switch pins 3 and 6 (TX).
Straight-Through vs. Crossover Cables:-

Straight-Through: pins are wired identically at both ends (1→1, 2→2, 3→3, 6→6). Used when connecting different device types — PC to Switch, Router to Switch — because TX pins on one device type align with RX pins on the other.

Crossover: pairs are swapped at one end (1→3, 2→6, 3→1, 6→2). Used when connecting the same device types — PC to PC, Switch to Switch, Router to Router — so that TX connects to RX rather than TX to TX.
[ Figure: Left: Straight-through — identical color pattern at both ends. Right: Crossover — orange and green pairs are swapped at one end. ]
Left: Straight-through — identical color pattern at both ends. Right: Crossover — orange and green pairs are swapped at one end.

Auto Medium Dependent Interface Crossover (Auto MDI-X): a feature on virtually all modern switches and routers that automatically detects the cable type and adjusts internally. Either cable type can be used in any situation — the device compensates automatically.
Gigabit and 10-Gigabit Ethernet:-

At speeds of 1 Gbps (1000BASE-T) and 10 Gbps (10GBASE-T), all 8 wires are used across all 4 pairs. Each pair operates bidirectionally — the same pair simultaneously carries signals in both directions using advanced signal processing. This bidirectionality enables the dramatically higher throughput.

blocks.text: Fiber Optic Cables:-

Fiber optic cables transmit data as pulses of light through a glass core, rather than electrical signals through copper. This enables much longer distances, higher speeds, and complete immunity to electromagnetic interference — making fiber the preferred medium for inter-building links, Wide Area Network (WAN) connections, and high-security environments.
Fiber Cable Structure (inside to outside):-
Fiberglass core: the medium through which light pulses travel.

Cladding: a glass layer surrounding the core with a different refractive index. This difference causes total internal reflection — light cannot escape through the cladding and stays confined to the core.
Buffer coating: a protective plastic layer that cushions the fragile glass.
Outer jacket: the tough outer sheath that protects the entire assembly from physical damage and the environment.
[ Figure: Fiber optic cable cross-section: fiberglass core → cladding → buffer coating → outer jacket. A light ray shown bouncing along the core via total internal reflection. ]
Fiber optic cable cross-section: fiberglass core → cladding → buffer coating → outer jacket. A light ray shown bouncing along the core via total internal reflection.
Small Form-factor Pluggable (SFP) Transceivers:-

Standard network device ports use electrical signals, so a fiber optic cable cannot be plugged directly into a regular Ethernet port. To connect a fiber cable to a switch or router, a Small Form-factor Pluggable (SFP) transceiver is required — a compact, hot-swappable module that slots into an SFP port on the device. The SFP converts the device's electrical signals into optical signals for transmission, and converts incoming light signals back into electrical signals.
Each fiber connection uses two separate strands — one for transmitting (TX) and one for receiving (RX) — making fiber connections inherently full-duplex.
[ Figure: SFP transceiver module plugging into a switch SFP port, with two fiber strands: one labeled TX and one labeled RX ]
SFP transceiver module plugging into a switch SFP port, with two fiber strands: one labeled TX and one labeled RX
Single-Mode vs. Multi-Mode Fiber:-

Multi-Mode Fiber (MMF): uses a Light Emitting Diode (LED) light source and a wider core (50 or 62.5 micrometers). Light bounces along multiple paths (modes), which causes slight signal spreading (modal dispersion) that limits distance to roughly 550 meters. Cheaper than single-mode. Best suited for short distances inside buildings or data centers.

Single-Mode Fiber (SMF): uses a laser light source and an extremely narrow core (9 micrometers). Light travels in a single straight path with virtually no dispersion, enabling distances of 100 kilometers or more. More expensive. Used for long-distance runs between buildings, campuses, and Wide Area Networks (WANs).
[ Figure: Left (Multi-Mode Fiber): wide core with multiple light rays bouncing. Right (Single-Mode Fiber): narrow core with a single straight laser beam — no bouncing, minimal dispersion. ]
Left (Multi-Mode Fiber): wide core with multiple light rays bouncing. Right (Single-Mode Fiber): narrow core with a single straight laser beam — no bouncing, minimal dispersion.

No signal leakage — cannot be passively tapped

blocks.text: Network Devices at Layer 1:-
Layer 1 devices operate purely on raw signals — they have no understanding of addresses or any higher-layer information. They simply receive a signal and retransmit it.

Hub: a basic Layer 1 device that connects multiple devices. When any device sends a signal, the hub amplifies and repeats it out of every other port with no intelligence about the intended destination. All devices share the same physical medium. Hubs are legacy technology replaced by switches.
Repeater: receives a signal, amplifies it to restore signal strength lost over distance, and retransmits it. Used to extend the maximum cable length of a network segment.
[ Figure: Hub: one device sends a signal → hub repeats it out every single port to all connected devices regardless of destination ]
Hub: one device sends a signal → hub repeats it out every single port to all connected devices regardless of destination
Frame Errors at Layer 1:-
Runt: a frame smaller than the minimum valid Ethernet frame size of 64 bytes. Typically caused by a collision or a malfunctioning network interface card (NIC).
Giant: a frame larger than the maximum valid Ethernet frame size of 1518 bytes (or 1522 bytes when an 802.1Q VLAN tag is present). Usually caused by a misconfigured device.
Layer 2: The Data Link Layer

Layer 1 defines how raw bits travel across a physical medium. Layer 2 organizes those bits into structured frames and ensures they reach the correct device on the local network. It introduces hardware addressing, error detection, and the intelligent devices — switches — that make selective forwarding possible.
Layer 2 Responsibilities:-
Framing: packages raw bits into structured units called frames, each with a defined start, hardware addressing, data payload, and error-check trailer.
Media Access Control (MAC) Addressing: every device has a unique hardware address. Layer 2 uses these addresses to identify the source and destination of each frame on the local network.
Error Detection: a checksum in the frame trailer lets the receiving device verify the frame arrived uncorrupted.
Media Access Control: on shared media, Layer 2 defines the rules for which device may transmit at any given moment to prevent signal collisions.
Note: Layer 2 only handles delivery between directly connected devices on the same local network. Delivering data across different networks is the job of Layer 3.
Switches — The Core Layer 2 Device:-

At Layer 1, a hub repeats every signal out of every port to every connected device — with no intelligence. If two devices transmit simultaneously, their signals collide on the shared medium and both transmissions are corrupted.

A switch is the intelligent Layer 2 replacement for the hub. A switch reads the destination Media Access Control (MAC) address of each incoming frame and forwards it only out the correct port — toward the intended recipient, not every device.
[ Figure: Left: Hub — device A sends, ALL devices receive. Right: Switch — device A sends to device B, only port B receives the frame. ]
Left: Hub — device A sends, ALL devices receive. Right: Switch — device A sends to device B, only port B receives the frame.
Collision Domains:-
A collision domain is a network segment where two devices transmitting simultaneously cause a collision. The type of device determines the collision domain boundaries:
Hub: all ports share one collision domain. Any two devices can collide with each other.
Switch: each port is its own isolated collision domain. Devices on different switch ports can transmit simultaneously without any collision.
[ Figure: Hub: one large shared collision domain enclosing all devices. Switch: each port is its own separate collision domain — no inter-port collisions. ]
Hub: one large shared collision domain enclosing all devices. Switch: each port is its own separate collision domain — no inter-port collisions.
Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD):-
When devices share a collision domain (as on a hub), they use Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD) to manage access to the shared medium:
Carrier Sense: before transmitting, a device listens to the medium to check that it is currently idle.
Multiple Access: multiple devices share the same physical medium.

Collision Detection: if two devices transmit simultaneously and a collision occurs, both immediately stop and broadcast a jamming signal to alert all devices. Each then waits a random back-off period before retrying.

Note: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD) only applies in half-duplex environments with shared collision domains. Modern switch-connected devices run full-duplex — CSMA/CD is disabled entirely.
Duplex Modes:-

Half-Duplex: a device can either send or receive at any moment — never both simultaneously. Requires Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD). Used with hubs and legacy equipment.
Full-Duplex: a device can send and receive simultaneously on separate wire pairs. No collisions are possible. All modern switch-connected devices operate in full-duplex.
Media Access Control (MAC) Addresses:-

Every network interface card (NIC) — in a laptop, phone, server, switch, or any networked device — has a Media Access Control (MAC) address permanently embedded by the manufacturer. The MAC address is how Layer 2 identifies devices on a local network.
48 bits long (6 bytes) — written as 12 hexadecimal characters, for example AA:BB:CC:11:22:33.
Burned-In Address (BIA): permanently written into the hardware at the factory. Cannot be changed by software, though it can be spoofed at the operating system level.
Globally unique: no two network interface cards in the world should share the same MAC address.
[ Figure: MAC address AA:BB:CC:11:22:33 — first 3 bytes (AA:BB:CC) highlighted as Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI), last 3 bytes (11:22:33) as unique device identifier ]
MAC address AA:BB:CC:11:22:33 — first 3 bytes (AA:BB:CC) highlighted as Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI), last 3 bytes (11:22:33) as unique device identifier

rows: Identifies the manufacturer. Every NIC made by Cisco shares the same OUI; Intel NICs share a different OUI.
Uniquely identifies this specific device within that manufacturer's product range.

blocks.text: The Ethernet Frame Structure:-

Ethernet is the dominant Layer 2 protocol in wired local area networks. When a Layer 3 packet arrives at Layer 2, it is wrapped in an Ethernet frame — a structured container with a header at the front and a trailer at the back.
[ Figure: Ethernet frame layout: [Preamble 7B | Start Frame Delimiter 1B | Destination MAC 6B | Source MAC 6B | Type/Length 2B | Payload 46–1500B | Frame Check Sequence 4B] ]
Ethernet frame layout: [Preamble 7B | Start Frame Delimiter 1B | Destination MAC 6B | Source MAC 6B | Type/Length 2B | Payload 46–1500B | Frame Check Sequence 4B]

rows: Alternating 1s and 0s (10101010 repeated). Allows receiving devices to synchronize their clock to the incoming bit stream before the actual frame begins.
The bit pattern 10101011. Signals the end of the preamble — the very next byte is the start of the Destination MAC Address field.
MAC address of the intended recipient. Can be unicast (one device), multicast (a group), or broadcast (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF — all devices on the local network).
MAC address of the sending device's network interface card (NIC).
Value 1536 (0x0600) or higher: identifies the Layer 3 protocol — 0x0800 = Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4), 0x86DD = IPv6. Value below 1536: indicates the byte length of the payload.

The encapsulated Layer 3 data — usually an IP packet (L3PDU). Minimum 46 bytes. If the actual data is shorter than 46 bytes, the switch appends padding bytes (zeros) to reach the minimum. This 64-byte minimum total frame size is required for correct collision detection on half-duplex links.
A Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) value. The receiver recalculates it — if it does not match, the frame was corrupted and is discarded.

blocks.text: Important: The Preamble and Start Frame Delimiter (SFD) are not counted in the Ethernet frame size. The 64-byte minimum applies from Destination MAC through Frame Check Sequence (FCS): 6 + 6 + 2 + 46 + 4 = 64 bytes.
MAC Address Table — Switch Learning and Forwarding:-

A switch maintains a MAC address table (also called a Content Addressable Memory (CAM) table) that maps each known MAC address to the switch port it was learned from. This table is built dynamically as frames arrive.
[ Figure: Switch learning: PC-A sends a frame with source MAC AA:BB:CC → switch records 'AA:BB:CC = Port 1' in its MAC table → switch looks up destination MAC → forwards only out the correct port ]
Switch learning: PC-A sends a frame with source MAC AA:BB:CC → switch records 'AA:BB:CC = Port 1' in its MAC table → switch looks up destination MAC → forwards only out the correct port
Learn: when a frame arrives, the switch reads the source MAC address and records it with the incoming port number in the MAC address table.

Forward: the switch looks up the destination MAC address. If found, the frame is sent only out that port (unicast forwarding). If not found, the frame is flooded out all ports except the one it arrived on — called unknown unicast flooding.
Aging: if a MAC address entry is not refreshed for 5 minutes, it is removed from the table. The switch will flood again until the address is relearned.
show mac address-table                              → view the full MAC address table
clear mac address-table dynamic                    → remove all dynamically learned entries
clear mac address-table dynamic address <MAC>      → remove one specific entry by MAC address
clear mac address-table dynamic interface <INT>    → remove all entries learned on one interface
VLANs and Trunking

All devices on a switch by default share the same local network and broadcast domain. Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) divide a single physical switch into multiple isolated logical networks. To carry traffic from multiple VLANs across one cable, switches use trunking.
Local Area Network (LAN) and Broadcast Domain:-
Local Area Network (LAN): a group of devices in a single location that are all part of the same network and can communicate directly at Layer 2.
Broadcast Domain: the set of all devices that receive a broadcast frame (destination MAC FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF) sent by any one member. By default, all ports on a switch are in the same broadcast domain.

Note: Routers break broadcast domains — a broadcast does not cross a router. Switches alone do not break broadcast domains, but Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) let you create multiple separate broadcast domains within a single switch.
Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs):-

A Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) logically separates end hosts at Layer 2 — creating isolated broadcast domains within a single physical switch. VLANs are configured per interface on the switch. A switch will not forward traffic directly between hosts in different VLANs; to communicate across VLANs, traffic must be routed at Layer 3, which is covered in the inter-VLAN routing section of the Layer 3 chapter.

[ Figure: One physical switch divided into 3 VLANs: VLAN 10 (Sales) on ports 1–4, VLAN 20 (Engineering) on ports 5–8, VLAN 30 (Management) on ports 9–12. A broadcast from VLAN 10 does not reach VLAN 20 or 30. ]
One physical switch divided into 3 VLANs: VLAN 10 (Sales) on ports 1–4, VLAN 20 (Engineering) on ports 5–8, VLAN 30 (Management) on ports 9–12. A broadcast from VLAN 10 does not reach VLAN 20 or 30.
Default VLANs:-
VLAN 1: the default VLAN. All switch interfaces belong to VLAN 1 by default. Also the default native VLAN on trunk ports. Cannot be deleted.
VLANs 1002, 1003, 1004, 1005: reserved for legacy Fiber Distributed Data Interface (FDDI) and Token Ring technologies. Cannot be used or deleted.

rows: Standard range. Supported on all Cisco switches and all VTP versions.

blocks.text: Configuring Access Ports:-
An access port belongs to exactly one VLAN and connects to end hosts such as PCs, printers, and servers. The end host is unaware of VLANs — the switch handles VLAN membership transparently.
int range g0/1 - 4               → select multiple interfaces at once
switchport mode access           → configure as an access port (also disables Dynamic Trunking Protocol)
switchport access vlan 10        → assign the port to VLAN 10 (auto-created if it does not exist)
vlan 10                          → enter VLAN configuration mode (creates VLAN 10 if needed)
name Sales                       → assign a descriptive name to the VLAN
show vlan brief                  → view all VLANs and which access ports belong to each
Note: 'show vlan brief' shows access ports only — trunk ports do not appear here. Use 'show interfaces trunk' to see trunk information.
Trunk Ports:-

A trunk port carries traffic from multiple Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) over a single physical cable. Trunk ports are used on switch-to-switch and switch-to-router links where traffic from many VLANs must travel on the same connection.
Access ports: untagged — carry traffic for a single VLAN. Connect to end hosts.
Trunk ports: tagged — carry traffic for multiple VLANs simultaneously. Connect to other switches or routers.

[ Figure: Two switches connected by a trunk link. VLAN 10, 20, and 30 traffic all travels on the same cable. Each frame is tagged with its VLAN ID so the receiving switch knows which VLAN it belongs to. ]
Two switches connected by a trunk link. VLAN 10, 20, and 30 traffic all travels on the same cable. Each frame is tagged with its VLAN ID so the receiving switch knows which VLAN it belongs to.
IEEE 802.1Q Trunking Protocol:-
Two trunking protocols exist: the old Cisco-proprietary Inter-Switch Link (ISL), and the modern industry-standard IEEE 802.1Q (dot1q). IEEE 802.1Q is universal and used in all modern networks.

When a switch sends a frame out a trunk port, it inserts a 4-byte IEEE 802.1Q tag into the Ethernet frame between the Source MAC Address and the Type/Length field. The receiving switch reads the tag to determine the VLAN, then strips it before delivering the frame to the destination host.
[ Figure: Ethernet frame with 802.1Q tag inserted between Source MAC and Type/Length: [Destination MAC | Source MAC | 802.1Q Tag 4B | Type/Length | Payload | FCS] ]
Ethernet frame with 802.1Q tag inserted between Source MAC and Type/Length: [Destination MAC | Source MAC | 802.1Q Tag 4B | Type/Length | Payload | FCS]

rows: Always 0x8100 — identifies this frame as 802.1Q tagged.
Class of Service (CoS) — used for Quality of Service (QoS) to prioritize delay-sensitive traffic such as voice.
If set to 1, this frame may be dropped first during network congestion.
Identifies the VLAN the frame belongs to. 12 bits = 4,096 possible values (0–4,095). VLANs 0 and 4,095 are reserved; usable range is 1–4,094.

blocks.text: Native VLAN:-

The native VLAN is an IEEE 802.1Q feature. Frames belonging to the native VLAN are sent across a trunk port without an 802.1Q tag — they travel as plain untagged frames. When a switch receives an untagged frame on a trunk port, it assumes the frame belongs to the native VLAN.
Default native VLAN: VLAN 1 on all trunk ports.
Must match: the native VLAN must be configured identically on both ends of a trunk link. A mismatch sends frames to the wrong VLAN.
Security best practice: change the native VLAN to an unused VLAN (such as VLAN 1001) to prevent VLAN hopping attacks.
Configuring Trunk Ports:-
int g0/1
switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q   → set encapsulation to IEEE 802.1Q (required on switches that support both ISL and dot1q)
switchport mode trunk                  → configure the port as a trunk
switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30 → restrict which VLANs are permitted on this trunk
switchport trunk native vlan 1001      → change native VLAN to an unused VLAN
show interfaces trunk                  → view trunk ports, allowed VLANs, and native VLAN
Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP):-

Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP) is a Cisco-proprietary protocol that allows Cisco switches to automatically negotiate whether an interface should be access or trunk — without manual configuration. It is enabled by default.

Security Warning: Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP) should be disabled on all switch ports. Automatic negotiation can be exploited to establish unauthorized trunk links. Always manually configure every port and disable DTP.

rows: Always a trunk. Sends DTP frames actively.
Actively tries to negotiate a trunk.
trunk, dynamic desirable, or dynamic auto.
Passively waits. Forms a trunk only if the peer actively initiates.
Always an access port. DTP negotiation disabled.

blocks.text: Older Cisco switches: default mode is dynamic desirable — actively try to form trunks.
Newer Cisco switches: default mode is dynamic auto — passively wait.
Non-Cisco devices: Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP) only works between Cisco switches. Ports connected to routers, PCs, or non-Cisco switches are always placed in access mode.
switchport nonegotiate    → disables DTP on the interface. Use after manually setting trunk or access mode.
Note: 'switchport mode access' automatically disables DTP. 'switchport mode trunk' does NOT — always add 'switchport nonegotiate' on trunk ports as well.
Trunk Encapsulation Negotiation:-

On switches that support both IEEE 802.1Q and Inter-Switch Link (ISL) encapsulation, Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP) can also negotiate which trunking encapsulation to use. The default trunk encapsulation mode on such switches is 'negotiate':
switchport trunk encapsulation negotiate   → default on switches that support both ISL and dot1q — DTP negotiates which to use
switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q       → explicitly set encapsulation to IEEE 802.1Q (recommended)

When encapsulation is set to negotiate, Inter-Switch Link (ISL) is preferred over IEEE 802.1Q — if both switches support ISL, it will be selected. Regarding DTP frame placement: DTP frames are sent in VLAN 1 when using Inter-Switch Link (ISL), or in the native VLAN when using IEEE 802.1Q (the default native VLAN is VLAN 1, so in practice both default to VLAN 1).

Best Practice: always set the trunk encapsulation explicitly with 'switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q' rather than relying on automatic negotiation. This ensures predictable behavior regardless of what the connected switch supports.
VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP):-

VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP) is a Cisco-proprietary protocol that distributes VLAN configuration from a central VTP server switch to all VTP client switches in the same domain — eliminating the need to configure VLANs individually on every switch.

Important: VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP) is rarely used in modern networks and is generally not recommended. A switch with a higher revision number can overwrite the VLAN database on all connected switches, potentially destroying the network configuration. Manual VLAN configuration per switch is the safer approach.

rows: Yes (if another server has a higher revision number)

blocks.text: Revision number: VTP servers increment this counter every time a VLAN is added, modified, or deleted. Clients always sync to the highest revision number. To safely reset it to zero: change the VTP domain name or switch the device to transparent mode.
VTP domain: all participating switches must use the same domain name. Command: vtp domain DOMAIN-NAME
Auto-join risk: a switch with no VTP domain (NULL) that receives a VTP advertisement automatically adopts that domain and revision number — a potential security risk.

VTP versions: VTPv1 and VTPv2 support only normal VLANs (1–1,005). VTPv3 adds support for extended VLANs (1,006–4,094). VTPv2 adds Token Ring VLAN support over VTPv1 but is otherwise nearly identical.
Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)

Network redundancy is critical — if one switch or link fails, traffic must continue through an alternate path. However, redundant Layer 2 links create loops, and loops are catastrophic in Ethernet networks. Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) automatically blocks redundant paths to prevent loops while keeping those paths on standby as instant backups.
The Problem with Redundant Links:-
Unlike Internet Protocol (IP) packets at Layer 3, Ethernet frames have no Time to Live (TTL) field — nothing naturally stops them from circulating forever in a loop.

Broadcast Storm: a broadcast frame (destination FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF) entering a loop is forwarded by every switch out every port indefinitely. Copies multiply rapidly. Within seconds, broadcast traffic consumes all available bandwidth and makes the network completely unusable.

MAC Address Flapping: in a loop, the same frame arrives on different switch ports repeatedly. The switch constantly updates its MAC address table, recording the same source MAC alternating between ports. This instability causes frames to be forwarded incorrectly and wastes switch resources.
[ Figure: Broadcast storm: Switch A, B, and C connected in a triangle. A broadcast frame enters → each switch forwards it out all ports → frames multiply and loop indefinitely. ]
Broadcast storm: Switch A, B, and C connected in a triangle. A broadcast frame enters → each switch forwards it out all ports → frames multiply and loop indefinitely.
STP Versions:-
Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) — IEEE 802.1D:-

Classic Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), defined in IEEE 802.1D, is enabled by default on switches from all vendors. STP prevents Layer 2 loops by placing selected ports into a blocking state — disabling them from forwarding regular traffic. Blocked ports act as standby links that can activate if the primary path fails.

rows: Normal operation — forwards all traffic and participates fully in Spanning Tree Protocol.
Discards all regular traffic. Listens for Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs) to detect topology changes. Activates if the active path fails.

blocks.text: Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs):-

Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) switches communicate using Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs). Hello BPDUs are sent out every interface every 2 seconds by default. If a switch receives a Hello BPDU on an interface, it knows that interface is connected to another switch — end hosts like PCs and routers do not send BPDUs.

rows: The original STP. All VLANs share one STP instance — cannot load balance.
Per-VLAN Spanning Tree. One STP instance per VLAN. Supports ISL trunking only.
Per-VLAN Spanning Tree Plus. One STP instance per VLAN. Supports IEEE 802.1Q trunking. Interoperates with IEEE 802.1D. Default on older Cisco switches.
Much faster convergence than 802.1D. All VLANs share one STP instance — cannot load balance.
Cisco's upgrade to 802.1w. One STP instance per VLAN. Supports IEEE 802.1Q. Can load balance. Default on modern Cisco switches.
Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol. Uses RSTP mechanics. Groups multiple VLANs into instances (e.g. VLANs 1–5 in instance 1, VLANs 6–10 in instance 2) to load balance.

blocks.text: Modern Cisco switches run Rapid PVST+ by default. To change the STP mode:
spanning-tree mode pvst            → classic Per-VLAN Spanning Tree Plus (PVST+)
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst      → Rapid PVST+ (default on modern Cisco switches)
Per-VLAN Spanning Tree Plus (PVST+) and STP Load Balancing:-

Cisco switches run Per-VLAN Spanning Tree Plus (PVST+) — a separate Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) instance runs independently for each VLAN. Different ports can be forwarding in VLAN 10 while blocking in VLAN 20. By assigning different root bridges per VLAN, traffic from different VLANs uses different physical paths — avoiding wasted redundant links and congestion on a single connection. This is called STP Load Balancing.
The Bridge ID:-
Every switch in an STP topology has a Bridge Identifier (Bridge ID) — a unique value used to elect the root bridge and make all forwarding decisions. The Bridge ID has two components:

Bridge Priority: compared first when electing the root bridge. Default is 32,768 on all switches. In Cisco's Per-VLAN Spanning Tree Plus (PVST+) implementation, this 16-bit field is split into a 4-bit Bridge Priority and a 12-bit Extended System ID (equal to the VLAN ID). So the default Bridge Priority in VLAN 1 is 32,768 + 1 = 32,769.
MAC Address: used as a tiebreaker when two switches have the same Bridge Priority. The switch with the numerically lower MAC address wins.
[ Figure: Bridge ID structure: [4-bit Bridge Priority | 12-bit Extended System ID (VLAN ID) | 48-bit MAC Address] — total 64 bits ]
Bridge ID structure: [4-bit Bridge Priority | 12-bit Extended System ID (VLAN ID) | 48-bit MAC Address] — total 64 bits

Because the Extended System ID (VLAN ID) cannot be changed, the Bridge Priority can only be adjusted in increments of 4,096. Valid values: 0, 4096, 8192, 12288, 16384, 20480, 24576, 28672, 32768, 36864, 40960, 45056, 49152, 53248, 57344, 61440. To manually set the priority and make a specific switch the root bridge — for example because it is more reliable or better positioned in the network:
spanning-tree vlan <vlan-id> priority <value>        → set a specific Bridge Priority (must be a multiple of 4096)
spanning-tree vlan <vlan-id> root primary            → shortcut: sets priority to 24,576 (or 4,096 less than the current lowest, whichever wins)
spanning-tree vlan <vlan-id> root secondary          → shortcut: sets priority to 28,672 — becomes root if the primary fails
Root Bridge Election:-

The first step of Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) is electing one switch as the root bridge — the reference point for the entire topology. All forwarding paths are calculated relative to the root bridge.

When a switch powers on, it assumes it is the root bridge and sends Hello BPDUs advertising itself. If it receives a BPDU from a switch with a lower Bridge ID, it gives up its claim. Once all switches agree, only the root bridge generates original BPDUs — all other switches only forward them.
Election rule: the switch with the lowest Bridge ID becomes the root bridge. Bridge Priority is compared first; if equal, the lower MAC address wins.
Root bridge ports: all ports on the root bridge are automatically Designated Ports in the forwarding state. The root bridge never has a blocking port.
[ Figure: STP election example: Switch A priority 32769, Switch B priority 32769, Switch C priority 4097. Switch C wins (lowest priority) → all Switch C ports become Designated and forwarding. ]
STP election example: Switch A priority 32769, Switch B priority 32769, Switch C priority 4097. Switch C wins (lowest priority) → all Switch C ports become Designated and forwarding.
STP Port Roles:-
After the root bridge is elected, every port in the network is assigned one of three roles:
Root Port:-

Every non-root switch selects exactly one Root Port — the port with the best path to the root bridge. Root ports are placed in the forwarding state. The port on the opposite end of every root port is always a Designated Port.
Tiebreaker order for root port selection:
Lowest Root Path Cost — the total cumulative cost of all links from this switch to the root bridge, based on link speed.
Lowest Neighbor Bridge ID — if costs are equal, prefer the port connected to the switch with the lower Bridge ID.

Lowest Neighbor Port ID — if the neighbor Bridge ID is also equal (e.g., two parallel links between the same switches), prefer the port connected to the neighbor's lower Port ID. Port ID = Port Priority (default 128) + Port Number. To influence which port a downstream switch selects as its root port, you can adjust the port priority on the upstream switch's interface: spanning-tree vlan <vlan-id> port-priority <value>
Note: It is the neighbor switch's Port ID that is used to break ties — not the local switch's own Port ID.
Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) Link Cost Values:-

Cost calculation example: Switch SW2 has two paths to the root bridge. Via G0/1: root bridge advertised cost 0, SW2's G0/1 link cost = 4 (1 Gbps), total = 4. Via G0/0: intermediate switch advertised cost 4, SW2's G0/0 adds 4, total = 8. SW2 selects G0/1 as its Root Port — lower total cost. To influence root port selection by adjusting the cost of a specific link:
spanning-tree vlan <vlan-id> cost <value>            → change the STP cost on this interface for the specified VLAN
Designated Port:-

Every network segment (every link between two switches) has exactly one Designated Port — the port that forwards traffic onto that segment. Designated ports are in the forwarding state. For links between two non-root switches, the designated port is chosen as follows:
The switch with the lower total root path cost makes its port the Designated Port.
If root path costs are equal: the switch with the lower Bridge ID makes its port the Designated Port.
The other switch's port becomes the Non-Designated (blocking) Port.
Non-Designated Port (Blocking):-

Any port that is neither a Root Port nor a Designated Port becomes a Non-Designated Port in the blocking state. This is the port STP disables to break the loop. It remains ready to transition to forwarding if the active path fails.
STP Decision Process — Summary:-
