STP Port States:-
Each switch port in a Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) topology is always in one of four states. Two are stable and two are transitional — passed through when changing from blocking to forwarding.

rows: Receives only — does NOT forward BPDUs
Indefinite — stays here until topology changes

blocks.text: Blocking State:-

Non-Designated ports remain stable in the Blocking state. A blocking port is effectively disabled to prevent loops — it does not send or receive regular network traffic, and it does not forward BPDUs. However, it does receive BPDUs so it can detect any change in the network topology. It does not learn MAC addresses — if regular traffic arrives on a blocking interface, it is dropped without updating the MAC address table.
Listening State:-

When a Blocking port must transition to Forwarding due to a topology change, it first enters the Listening state. Only ports with a Designated or Root role enter the Listening state — Non-Designated ports always remain Blocking. The Listening state lasts 15 seconds by default (Forward Delay timer). The port only sends and receives BPDUs — no regular traffic is forwarded and no MAC addresses are learned.
Learning State:-

After the Listening state, a Designated or Root port enters the Learning state — also 15 seconds long, using the same Forward Delay timer. The port still does not forward regular traffic, but it now learns MAC addresses. This allows the switch to build its MAC address table before the port starts forwarding, reducing unnecessary flooding.
Forwarding State:-

Root Ports and Designated Ports remain stable in the Forwarding state — normal operation. A Forwarding port sends and receives both BPDUs and regular traffic, and learns MAC addresses. Only switches forward BPDUs out of their Designated ports.

Note: A Forwarding port can move directly to Blocking with no delay — blocking cannot create a loop. However, a Blocking port must always pass through Listening (15 s) and Learning (15 s) first — 30 seconds total — before reaching Forwarding. This prevents loops from accidentally forming. A blocking interface transitioning after Max Age expires takes 50 seconds total (20 s Max Age + 15 s Listening + 15 s Learning).
STP Timers:-

rows: How often the root bridge sends Hello BPDUs. All other switches only forward these BPDUs.
How long a port spends in the Listening state, then the Learning state (15 s each = 30 s total before Forwarding).

How long an interface waits after ceasing to receive Hello BPDUs before re-evaluating the STP topology. Resets every time a BPDU is received. If it reaches 0, the switch re-elects the root bridge, root ports, and designated ports. 20 seconds = 10 × Hello interval.

blocks.text: STP Toolkit:-
The STP Toolkit refers to a set of features that enhance, protect, and optimize Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) behavior: PortFast, BPDU Guard, BPDU Filter, Root Guard, and Loop Guard.
PortFast:-

PortFast allows a switch port to skip the Listening and Learning states and move immediately to the Forwarding state when it becomes active. This removes the 30-second delay that would otherwise occur when a device first connects.
Use only on ports connected to end hosts (PCs, servers, printers) — never on ports connected to other switches. Enabling PortFast on a switch-to-switch port could create a Layer 2 loop.
int g#/#
spanning-tree portfast                         → enable PortFast on this interface
spanning-tree portfast trunk                   → enable PortFast on a trunk interface (use with caution)
spanning-tree portfast disable                 → disable PortFast on this specific port
To enable PortFast globally on all access ports (not trunk ports):
spanning-tree portfast default                 → enables PortFast on all access ports automatically
BPDU Guard:-

BPDU Guard protects PortFast-enabled ports from accidentally receiving Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs). If a BPDU Guard-enabled port receives a BPDU — indicating another switch has been connected — the port is immediately shut down (placed in an ErrDisable state) to prevent a potential loop.
int g#/#
spanning-tree bpduguard enable                 → enable BPDU Guard on this interface
To enable BPDU Guard globally on all PortFast-enabled interfaces:
spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default        → enables BPDU Guard on all PortFast ports
ErrDisable and ErrDisable Recovery:-

ErrDisable is a Cisco switch feature that automatically shuts down a port when a policy violation is detected — such as a BPDU Guard violation. The port enters an err-disabled state and stops forwarding traffic.
To re-enable an err-disabled port, the underlying issue must be fixed first. Re-enabling without fixing the cause will immediately err-disable the port again. There are two ways to re-enable:
Manual: enter interface configuration mode and use 'shutdown' followed by 'no shutdown' to reset the port.
Automatic — ErrDisable Recovery: automatically re-enables err-disabled ports after a configurable timer expires. Disabled by default.
errdisable recovery cause bpduguard                     → enable automatic recovery for BPDU Guard violations
errdisable recovery interval <seconds>                  → set the recovery timer (default is 300 seconds / 5 minutes)
show errdisable recovery                                → view ErrDisable Recovery status and timers
BPDU Filter:-

BPDU Filter prevents a port from sending Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs). Unlike BPDU Guard, it does not disable the port if it receives a BPDU. Useful on ports connected to end hosts where sending BPDUs wastes bandwidth and exposes STP topology information unnecessarily. BPDU Filter can be configured in two ways:
Per-port (use with caution): the port will not send BPDUs and will ignore any BPDUs it receives. This effectively disables STP on the port entirely.
spanning-tree bpdufilter enable
Default (recommended): enables BPDU Filter on all PortFast-enabled ports. If the port receives a BPDU, PortFast and BPDU Filter are automatically disabled and the port operates as a normal STP port.
spanning-tree portfast [edge] bpdufilter default        → enable BPDU Filter on all PortFast-enabled ports
Root Guard:-

Root Guard protects the STP topology by preventing an unauthorized switch from becoming the root bridge. When enabled on an interface, if that interface receives a superior BPDU — one with a lower Bridge ID than the current root bridge — the port is placed into a Broken (Root Inconsistent) state, effectively disabling it.
A good practice is to enable Root Guard on all ports connecting to switches outside of your administrative control.
int g#/#
spanning-tree guard root                               → enable Root Guard on this interface

A Root Guard-disabled port will not forward data frames and will discard any frames it receives. Once the superior BPDUs stop being received and their Max Age (20 seconds by default) expires, the port is automatically re-enabled.
Loop Guard:-

Loop Guard protects against unidirectional link failures — where data flows in only one direction between two switches. This is more common with fiber optic cables than copper UTP, due to the separate TX and RX strands. Causes include damaged cables, faulty connectors, or faulty SFP transceivers.

Without Loop Guard, if a Root or Non-Designated port stops receiving BPDUs due to a unidirectional failure, the Max Age timer eventually expires and the port transitions to Forwarding — potentially creating a loop. Loop Guard prevents this by placing the port into a Broken (Loop Inconsistent) state instead. The port remains up/up physically but STP blocks it. If BPDUs are received again, the port is automatically re-enabled.
Loop Guard should be enabled on: Root Ports and Non-Designated Ports — ports that are supposed to be receiving BPDUs.
spanning-tree guard loop                               → enable Loop Guard on a specific interface
spanning-tree loopguard default                        → enable Loop Guard on all ports globally
spanning-tree guard none                               → disable Loop Guard on a specific port
Root Guard vs. Loop Guard:-
Root Guard and Loop Guard are mutually exclusive — they cannot both be enabled on the same port. Their purposes are opposite:
Root Guard: applied to Designated Ports — prevents them from becoming Root Ports by blocking superior BPDUs.
Loop Guard: applied to Root and Non-Designated Ports — prevents them from becoming Designated Ports when BPDUs stop arriving.

If both are configured on the same port, the more specific configuration wins. If Loop Guard is enabled globally and Root Guard is then configured on a specific port, Root Guard takes effect on that port and Loop Guard is disabled there.

[ Figure: STP Toolkit summary: PortFast on edge/access ports → BPDU Guard protects those ports → Root Guard on designated ports facing untrusted switches → Loop Guard on root/non-designated ports facing unidirectional link risk ]

STP Toolkit summary: PortFast on edge/access ports → BPDU Guard protects those ports → Root Guard on designated ports facing untrusted switches → Loop Guard on root/non-designated ports facing unidirectional link risk
Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (RSTP) — IEEE 802.1w:-

Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (RSTP), standardized as IEEE 802.1w and implemented in Cisco switches as Rapid PVST+, is the modern replacement for Classic STP. Its key advantage is dramatically faster convergence — adapting to topology changes in seconds rather than up to 50 seconds with Classic STP.
RSTP Port States:-
Rapid STP simplifies the port states compared to Classic STP. The Listening state is removed entirely, and the Disabled and Blocking states are merged into a single Discarding state:

rows: Port is enabled but blocking traffic to prevent loops.
The Listening state does not exist in RSTP.
Same as Classic STP — learns MAC addresses but does not forward traffic.
Same as Classic STP — fully operational.

blocks.text: Note: Classic STP (IEEE 802.1D) uses destination MAC address 0180.C200.0000 for BPDUs. Cisco's PVST+ uses 0100.0CCC.CCCD. Rapid STP is backward compatible with Classic STP — interfaces connected to a Classic STP switch will automatically operate in Classic STP mode, reverting to the full Blocking → Listening → Learning → Forwarding process with the original timers.
RSTP Port Roles:-
Rapid STP retains the Root Port and Designated Port roles from Classic STP, but splits the Non-Designated port role into two distinct roles:

Alternate Port: a Discarding port that receives a superior BPDU from another switch. It is the best alternative path to the root bridge. If the Root Port fails, the Alternate Port can move immediately to Forwarding without waiting — this is equivalent to the classic optional UplinkFast feature, but is built into RSTP automatically.

Backup Port: a Discarding port that receives a superior BPDU from another interface on the same switch. This only occurs when two interfaces on the same switch are connected to the same collision domain (via a hub). Hubs are not used in modern networks, so this role is rarely seen. The interface with the lowest Port ID becomes the Designated Port; the other becomes the Backup Port.
RSTP BPDU Behavior:-

In Classic STP, only the root bridge originates BPDUs — all other switches simply forward the BPDUs they receive. In Rapid STP, every switch originates and sends its own BPDUs from its Designated ports every Hello interval (2 seconds by default).

RSTP also ages out neighbor information much faster. Classic STP waits 10 Hello intervals (20 seconds — the Max Age timer) before considering a neighbor lost. Rapid STP considers a neighbor lost if it misses 3 consecutive BPDUs (6 seconds). When a neighbor is considered lost, the switch immediately flushes all MAC addresses learned on that interface.
RSTP Link Types:-

Rapid STP classifies each port into one of three link types, which determines how quickly it can transition to Forwarding. The link type is detected automatically, but can also be manually configured when needed:

Edge: a port connected directly to an end host (PC, server, printer). Moves immediately to Forwarding without negotiation — equivalent to Classic STP's PortFast. Configured with: spanning-tree portfast. Edge ports are built into RSTP automatically.
Point-to-Point: a direct full-duplex connection between two switches. RSTP can rapidly negotiate Forwarding using a handshake process. Detected automatically in full-duplex.
Shared: a connection to a hub operating in half-duplex. Must use Classic STP timers and transition process. Detected automatically in half-duplex.
To manually override the detected link type when needed:
spanning-tree link-type <point-to-point|shared>       → manually set the link type on this interface

Note: Two Classic STP optional features — UplinkFast (fast failover for Root Ports) and BackboneFast (fast recovery from indirect failures) — are both built into RSTP automatically. You do not need to configure them separately when using Rapid PVST+.
Viewing STP Information:-
show spanning-tree                       → view STP state for all VLANs, including port roles and states
show spanning-tree vlan <vlan-id>        → filter by a specific VLAN
show spanning-tree detail                → detailed view including total path cost to the root bridge
show spanning-tree summary               → lists each VLAN and the number of interfaces in each STP state
show spanning-tree interface g#/# detail → detailed STP information for a specific interface
EtherChannel

When multiple links connect two switches, Spanning Tree Protocol disables all but one to prevent loops — leaving redundant bandwidth unused. EtherChannel bundles multiple physical interfaces together into a single logical interface, allowing all links to carry traffic simultaneously while STP sees only one connection.
Network Design Context:-
In a typical campus network, there are two important switch roles:
Access Layer Switch: the switch that end hosts (PCs, phones, printers) connect directly to. This is the edge of the network.
Distribution Layer Switch: the switch that access layer switches connect to. It aggregates traffic from multiple access switches and connects them to the rest of the network or the internet.

When the total bandwidth of all end-host-facing interfaces on an access switch exceeds the uplink bandwidth to the distribution switch, this is called oversubscription. Some oversubscription is acceptable, but too much causes congestion.

Connecting two switches with multiple links without EtherChannel causes Spanning Tree Protocol to block all links except one — the redundant links carry no traffic unless the active link fails. EtherChannel solves this by making STP treat the entire bundle as a single interface, allowing all physical links to forward simultaneously.
[ Figure: Two switches connected by 4 physical links: without EtherChannel, STP blocks 3 of them. With EtherChannel, all 4 links are active and treated as one logical interface by STP. ]
Two switches connected by 4 physical links: without EtherChannel, STP blocks 3 of them. With EtherChannel, all 4 links are active and treated as one logical interface by STP.
How EtherChannel Works:-

EtherChannel (also called Port Channel or Link Aggregation Group (LAG)) groups multiple physical interfaces into one logical interface. Traffic is distributed across the physical links using a load-balancing algorithm based on flows — a flow being a communication between two specific nodes.

All frames belonging to the same flow are always sent over the same physical interface. This guarantees in-order delivery within each flow. Sending frames from the same flow over different physical interfaces could cause out-of-order arrival, which causes problems for higher-layer protocols.
Load-Balancing Methods:-
The EtherChannel load-balancing algorithm selects which physical interface to use based on a hash of one or more packet fields. The available inputs are:
src-mac: source MAC address.
dst-mac: destination MAC address.
src-dst-mac: source and destination MAC addresses (default on many switches).
src-ip: source IP address.
dst-ip: destination IP address.
src-dst-ip: source and destination IP addresses.
port-channel load-balance <method>          → change the load-balancing method (global config mode)
show etherchannel load-balance              → view the current load-balancing method
EtherChannel Configuration Methods:-
There are three methods for forming an EtherChannel on Cisco switches:
1 — Port Aggregation Protocol (PAgP):-

Port Aggregation Protocol (PAgP) is a Cisco-proprietary protocol that dynamically negotiates the creation and maintenance of an EtherChannel — similar to how Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP) works for trunks.

rows: No — both are passive, neither initiates

blocks.text: 2 — Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP):-

Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) is the industry-standard protocol (IEEE 802.3ad) for dynamic EtherChannel negotiation. It is equivalent to PAgP but works between switches from different vendors.

rows: No — both are passive, neither initiates

blocks.text: Note: LACP supports up to 16 interfaces in a single EtherChannel, but only 8 can be active at once. The remaining 8 are in standby mode, ready to become active if one of the active interfaces fails.
3 — Static EtherChannel:-

Static EtherChannel does not use any negotiation protocol. Interfaces are manually configured to form an EtherChannel. Both sides must be set to 'on' mode. On mode only works with on mode — mixing 'on' with 'desirable' (PAgP) or 'active' (LACP) will not form an EtherChannel.
Configuring EtherChannel:-
The configuration steps are the same regardless of the protocol used — only the mode name differs:
int range g0/0 - 3                         → select all interfaces to include in the EtherChannel
channel-group <number> mode <mode>          → assign interfaces to a channel group with the chosen mode
Mode options: desirable or auto (PAgP) | active or passive (LACP) | on (Static).
channel-protocol <pagp|lacp>               → optionally specify the protocol (not required — the mode implies the protocol)

Note: The channel-group number must match across all member interfaces on the same switch. However, it does not need to match the channel-group number on the other switch — channel-group 1 on Switch A can form an EtherChannel with channel-group 2 on Switch B.
Member Interface Requirements:-
All interfaces in an EtherChannel must have identical configurations. If any interface has a mismatching configuration, it is excluded from the EtherChannel. Matching requirements:
Same duplex mode (full or half).
Same speed.
Same switchport mode (all access or all trunk).
Same allowed VLANs and native VLAN (for trunk interfaces).
Verifying EtherChannel:-
show ip interface brief                     → the Port-Channel interface appears as a single logical interface
show etherchannel summary                   → view all EtherChannels, member interfaces, and their status
show etherchannel port-channel              → detailed view of each port-channel interface
show etherchannel load-balance              → confirm the current load-balancing method
Layer 3 EtherChannel:-

EtherChannel can also be used on Layer 3 (multilayer) switches. Instead of carrying switched traffic, the port-channel interface is configured as a routed Layer 3 interface with an IP address. Because Layer 3 routing does not rely on broadcasts in the same way as Layer 2 switching, Spanning Tree Protocol is not required for Layer 3 EtherChannels.
int range g0/0 - 3
no switchport                               → convert interfaces to Layer 3 routed ports
channel-group <number> mode <mode>          → form the EtherChannel
int port-channel <number>
no switchport                               → ensure the port-channel itself is a routed interface
ip address <ip-address> <subnet-mask>       → assign IP address to the logical EtherChannel interface
Layer 3: The Network Layer

Layer 2 delivers frames between devices on the same local network. Layer 3 makes communication possible between devices on completely different networks — anywhere in the world. It introduces IP addresses, routers, and the logic needed to find the best path from any source to any destination.
Network Devices at Layer 3 — Routers:-

A router is the primary Layer 3 device. Its job is to receive packets, examine the destination Internet Protocol (IP) address, and forward each packet out the correct interface toward its destination — hop by hop across the network. Routers connect different networks to each other, enabling global communication that Layer 2 switches cannot provide.
Layer 3 has three core responsibilities, all performed by routers:

Logical Addressing: Internet Protocol (IP) addresses uniquely identify every device across any network in the world — unlike MAC addresses, which are only meaningful within a single local network. IP addresses stay the same end-to-end from source to destination, while MAC addresses change at every single hop.
Routing: routers examine the destination IP address of each packet and forward it along the best available path across the network.

Encapsulation: at each hop, the router strips the incoming Layer 2 frame (L2PDU), reads the Layer 3 IP address, makes a routing decision, then re-encapsulates the packet (L3PDU) in a brand new Layer 2 frame for the next link. The IP header — added at Layer 3 and containing source and destination IP addresses — is what the router uses to make these decisions.

[ Figure: Packet traveling through 2 routers: Source → Router 1 (strips L2 frame, reads IP, creates new L2 frame) → Router 2 (same process) → Destination. IP addresses unchanged throughout; MAC addresses change at every hop. ]

Packet traveling through 2 routers: Source → Router 1 (strips L2 frame, reads IP, creates new L2 frame) → Router 2 (same process) → Destination. IP addresses unchanged throughout; MAC addresses change at every hop.
Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) Addressing:-

Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) is the most widely used Layer 3 protocol. An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number written in dotted-decimal notation — four groups of 8 bits (called octets) separated by dots.
[ Figure: IPv4 address 192.168.1.100 shown across four 8-bit octets in binary. Subnet mask 255.255.255.0 (/24) below it, with the network/host boundary between the 3rd and 4th octets. ]
IPv4 address 192.168.1.100 shown across four 8-bit octets in binary. Subnet mask 255.255.255.0 (/24) below it, with the network/host boundary between the 3rd and 4th octets.
Network Portion and Host Portion:-
A subnet mask divides an IPv4 address into two parts:
Network portion: identifies which network the device belongs to. All devices on the same network share an identical network portion.
Host portion: identifies the specific device within that network. Must be unique within the network.
Example: 192.168.1.100 with mask /24 (255.255.255.0) — network portion: 192.168.1, host portion: .100.
Special IPv4 Addresses:-
Network Address (host portion all zeros — e.g., 192.168.1.0/24): represents the network itself. Used in routing tables to refer to the entire subnet. Cannot be assigned to a host.
Broadcast Address (host portion all ones — e.g., 192.168.1.255/24): a packet sent here is delivered to every host in the subnet. Cannot be assigned to a host.
Loopback Range (127.0.0.0–127.255.255.255): reserved for testing the local device's own TCP/IP stack. Traffic never leaves the device. The most commonly used loopback address is 127.0.0.1.
Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR):-
Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) replaced the older classful networking system to prevent the rapid exhaustion of IPv4 addresses. The classful system assigned addresses in rigid fixed sizes:

rows: 16,777,214 hosts — far too large for most organizations
65,534 hosts — still too large for most

blocks.text: The problem: a company needing 2,000 host addresses would receive an entire Class B network (65,534 hosts) — wasting over 63,000 addresses. Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) allows any prefix length. That same company could receive a /21 network (2,046 usable hosts) — a far more efficient allocation. CIDR is now universal in all modern networking.
Subnet Masks — Fixed-Length and Variable-Length:-

Fixed-Length Subnet Masks (FLSM): all subnets use the same prefix length and therefore the same number of host addresses. Simple to design but inefficient when subnets have very different size requirements.

Variable-Length Subnet Masks (VLSM): different subnets use different prefix lengths, allowing each subnet to be exactly sized for its actual needs. A subnet for 100 hosts uses /25 (126 usable hosts); a point-to-point link uses /30 (2 usable hosts). Variable-Length Subnet Masks (VLSM) is the standard approach in modern network design.

rows: High — if some subnets only need 10 hosts, 52 addresses per subnet are wasted
Each sized to actual need (e.g., /28 = 14 hosts, /30 = 2 hosts)

blocks.text: IPv4 Packet Header:-
When a Layer 4 segment or datagram arrives at Layer 3, an IP header is added to create an IP packet. Every field in the header serves a specific purpose.

[ Figure: IPv4 header field layout with bit widths: Version (4) | IHL (4) | DSCP (6) | ECN (2) | Total Length (16) | Identification (16) | Flags (3) | Fragment Offset (13) | TTL (8) | Protocol (8) | Header Checksum (16) | Source IP (32) | Destination IP (32) | Options (variable) ]

IPv4 header field layout with bit widths: Version (4) | IHL (4) | DSCP (6) | ECN (2) | Total Length (16) | Identification (16) | Flags (3) | Fragment Offset (13) | TTL (8) | Protocol (8) | Header Checksum (16) | Source IP (32) | Destination IP (32) | Options (variable)

rows: Length of the IP header in 32-bit words. Minimum = 5 (5 × 4 = 20 bytes, no options). Maximum = 15 (60 bytes, with options present).
Used for Quality of Service (QoS) — allows routers to prioritize delay-sensitive traffic such as voice calls and video.
Allows routers to signal network congestion to endpoints without dropping packets. Requires all devices along the path to support it.
Total size of the IP packet in bytes (header + payload). Minimum = 20 bytes. Maximum = 65,535 bytes.
A unique value per original packet. When fragmented, all fragments of the same packet share this value for reassembly.

Bit 0: Reserved (always 0). Bit 1: Don't Fragment (DF) — if set, routers must not fragment this packet; if too large, it is dropped and an ICMP error is returned. Bit 2: More Fragments (MF) — set to 1 on all fragments except the last.
Position (in 8-byte units) of this fragment within the original packet. Allows correct reassembly even if fragments arrive out of order.

A hop counter decremented by 1 at each router. When it reaches 0, the router drops the packet and sends an ICMP 'Time Exceeded' message to the source. Prevents packets from looping indefinitely. Recommended default: 64.

Identifies the Layer 4 protocol in the payload: 1 = Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), 6 = Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), 17 = User Datagram Protocol (UDP), 89 = Open Shortest Path First (OSPF).
Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) covering the IP header only — not the payload. Recalculated at every router because the Time to Live (TTL) changes each hop. A mismatch causes the packet to be dropped.
IP address of the original sender. Does not change as the packet travels through the network.
IP address of the final destination. Routers use this field to make every forwarding decision.
Optional, variable-length field. Rarely used in practice. Present only when Internet Header Length (IHL) is greater than 5.

blocks.text: Important: The Header Checksum protects only the IP header — not the payload data. Payload error detection is the responsibility of Layer 4: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and User Datagram Protocol (UDP) each have their own checksum fields.
IP Fragmentation:-

Every network link has a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) — the largest packet it can carry. For standard Ethernet, the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) is 1,500 bytes. If an IP packet exceeds the MTU of a link, the router fragments it. The receiving host — not intermediate routers — reassembles the fragments using the Identification, Flags, and Fragment Offset fields.
Time to Live (TTL) and Routing Loops:-

Without the Time to Live (TTL) field, a packet caught in a routing loop would circulate forever. Starting at 64 (recommended default), TTL is decremented by 1 at each router. When it reaches 0, the packet is dropped and an Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) 'Time Exceeded' error is returned to the source. This mechanism also underpins traceroute — which intentionally sends packets with TTL = 1, 2, 3, and so on to map the hops along a path.
Address Resolution Protocol (ARP):-

Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) operates at the boundary between Layer 2 and Layer 3. When a device knows the destination Internet Protocol (IP) address but needs the destination Media Access Control (MAC) address to build an Ethernet frame (L2PDU), ARP discovers that MAC address automatically.

[ Figure: ARP flow: PC-A knows destination IP 192.168.1.20 but not its MAC → broadcasts ARP Request (Who has 192.168.1.20?) to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF → PC-B replies with unicast ARP Reply containing its MAC address ]
ARP flow: PC-A knows destination IP 192.168.1.20 but not its MAC → broadcasts ARP Request (Who has 192.168.1.20?) to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF → PC-B replies with unicast ARP Reply containing its MAC address

rows: Device that needs the MAC address
Broadcast — FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF (all devices on the local network receive it)
"Who has IP address X.X.X.X? Please reply with your MAC address."
Device that owns that IP address
Unicast — sent directly to the MAC address of the requesting device
"I have IP address X.X.X.X. My MAC address is AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF."

blocks.text: After the ARP Reply is received, the IP-to-MAC mapping is stored in the ARP table (also called the ARP cache). Entries expire after a period of inactivity so the table stays current as addresses change.
Static ARP entry: manually configured, permanent — does not expire. Used for security-sensitive or critical devices.
Dynamic ARP entry: learned automatically via Address Resolution Protocol (ARP). Expires after inactivity.
When reading ARP table output, the column labels use the following terminology:
Internet Address / Logical Address: refers to the IP address of the device.
Physical Address: refers to the MAC address of the device.
Type — Static: a default system entry or a manually configured entry.
Type — Dynamic: an entry learned automatically via Address Resolution Protocol (ARP).
arp -a          → Windows, Linux, macOS: view the ARP table
show arp        → Cisco IOS: view the ARP table (shows IP address, MAC address, interface, and entry type)
The Ping Utility:-

Ping is a network diagnostic tool that tests whether a destination is reachable and measures the round-trip time (RTT). It uses Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) — sending an ICMP Echo Request to the destination and waiting for an ICMP Echo Reply. A successful reply confirms the path is working end-to-end.
ICMP Echo Request: sent by the initiating device to the target IP address.
ICMP Echo Reply: sent back by the target device if it is reachable.

Note: When pinging a device on the same subnet for the first time, Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) must run first to resolve the destination MAC address. Only then can the ICMP packet be encapsulated in an Ethernet frame and sent. This is why the very first ping can occasionally be slow or fail.
The Routing Table:-
A router consults its routing table for every forwarding decision — a database mapping destination networks to the interface or next-hop address used to reach them. To view it on a Cisco router:
show ip route
The output shows a codes legend at the top listing all the protocols the router can use to learn routes, followed by the actual routing table entries.
Route Codes — How Routes Are Learned:-

L — Local: a route to the exact IP address configured on this router's own interface. Uses a /32 prefix (e.g., 192.168.1.1/32) — the /32 mask has no host bits, matching exactly this one specific address.
C — Connected: a route to the network the interface is directly part of. Uses the actual configured subnet prefix (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24 — the entire subnet).
S — Static: a route manually configured by a network administrator using the 'ip route' command.
O — OSPF: a route learned from a neighboring router via the Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) dynamic routing protocol.

Note: When you configure an IP address on an interface and enable it with 'no shutdown', two routes are automatically added: one Local (L) route for the interface's exact IP, and one Connected (C) route for the subnet. These appear automatically — they are neither static nor dynamic.
Types of Routing:-

Dynamic Routing: routers automatically exchange routing information with neighboring routers and build their tables without manual intervention. When the network changes, routers update their tables automatically. Examples: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF), Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP), Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). Scales well for large networks.

Static Routing: a network engineer manually configures routes using the 'ip route' command. The router only knows what it is explicitly told and does not adapt automatically to topology changes. Appropriate for small networks or specific fixed routes.
Configuring Static Routes:-
Static routes are added to the routing table using the 'ip route' command. Three methods exist:
Method 1 — Next-Hop IP Address: specify the IP address of the next router in the path.
ip route <destination-network> <subnet-mask> <next-hop-ip>
Method 2 — Exit Interface: specify which local interface the packet should leave through.
ip route <destination-network> <subnet-mask> <exit-interface>
Example: ip route 10.0.0.0 255.255.255.0 GigabitEthernet0/0
Method 3 — Both (recommended): specify both the exit interface and the next-hop IP address.
ip route <destination-network> <subnet-mask> <exit-interface> <next-hop-ip>
Example: ip route 10.0.0.0 255.255.255.0 GigabitEthernet0/0 192.168.1.2
Default Route — Gateway of Last Resort:-
A default route is a catch-all route that matches any destination IP address that does not match a more specific entry in the routing table.
Notation: 0.0.0.0/0 — both the network address and mask are all zeros. This matches every possible destination when no more specific route exists.
Behavior: when a router has no specific match for a packet's destination, it forwards using the default route. Without one, unmatched packets are dropped.
Common use: sending all internet-bound traffic toward the Internet Service Provider (ISP). Home routers use exactly this — a single default route handles all outbound internet traffic.
Terminology: called the Default Gateway on end hosts (PCs, servers); called the Gateway of Last Resort on routers, as shown in 'show ip route' output.
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 <next-hop-ip>     → configure a default route
[ Figure: 'show ip route' output: 'Gateway of last resort is X.X.X.X to network 0.0.0.0' at the top, C and L routes for connected interfaces, S* for the default static route. ]
'show ip route' output: 'Gateway of last resort is X.X.X.X to network 0.0.0.0' at the top, C and L routes for connected interfaces, S* for the default static route.
Inter-VLAN Routing:-
Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) create isolated Layer 2 broadcast domains. For hosts in different VLANs to communicate, their traffic must be routed at Layer 3. There are two main approaches:
Router on a Stick (ROAS):-

Router on a Stick (ROAS) routes between multiple VLANs using a single physical router interface connected to a trunk port on the switch. The router's physical interface is divided into logical subinterfaces — one per VLAN — each configured with its own IP address, which becomes the default gateway for hosts in that VLAN.

[ Figure: ROAS topology: Switch trunk port connects to Router G0/0. Router G0/0 is divided into subinterfaces: G0/0.10 (VLAN 10 gateway 192.168.10.1), G0/0.20 (VLAN 20 gateway 192.168.20.1), G0/0.30 (VLAN 30 gateway 192.168.30.1). ]

ROAS topology: Switch trunk port connects to Router G0/0. Router G0/0 is divided into subinterfaces: G0/0.10 (VLAN 10 gateway 192.168.10.1), G0/0.20 (VLAN 20 gateway 192.168.20.1), G0/0.30 (VLAN 30 gateway 192.168.30.1).
int g0/0.10                               → create subinterface for VLAN 10
encapsulation dot1q 10                    → handle frames tagged with VLAN 10
ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0     → default gateway IP for VLAN 10 hosts
Repeat for each VLAN. For the native VLAN, two options exist:
Option 1: use a subinterface and add the 'native' keyword: encapsulation dot1q 1001 native
Option 2: configure the IP directly on the physical interface — native VLAN frames arrive untagged, so no encapsulation command is needed.

Note: Router on a Stick (ROAS) creates a bottleneck — all inter-VLAN traffic must travel through one physical cable to the router and back. For larger or higher-traffic networks, a Layer 3 (multilayer) switch is the preferred solution.
Layer 3 / Multilayer Switches:-

A multilayer switch (also called a Layer 3 switch) can both switch at Layer 2 and route at Layer 3. Inter-VLAN routing happens inside the switch itself at wire speed — eliminating the ROAS bottleneck entirely.
Instead of an external router, each VLAN gets a Switch Virtual Interface (SVI) — a virtual Layer 3 interface on the switch that acts as the default gateway for hosts in that VLAN.
[ Figure: Multilayer switch: VLAN 10 hosts → SVI for VLAN 10 (192.168.10.1) → routed internally → SVI for VLAN 20 (192.168.20.1) → VLAN 20 hosts. No external router needed. ]
Multilayer switch: VLAN 10 hosts → SVI for VLAN 10 (192.168.10.1) → routed internally → SVI for VLAN 20 (192.168.20.1) → VLAN 20 hosts. No external router needed.
ip routing                                 → enable Layer 3 routing on the switch
To configure a routed uplink port (connecting to an external router):
int g0/1
no switchport                              → convert from Layer 2 switch port to Layer 3 routed port
ip address 192.168.1.2 255.255.255.0       → assign IP to the routed port
To create Switch Virtual Interfaces (SVIs) as default gateways:
int vlan 10
ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0      → this IP is the default gateway for all VLAN 10 hosts
int vlan 20
ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0      → default gateway for VLAN 20 hosts
Cisco IOS — Interface Status:-
show ip interface brief
[ Figure: Example output of 'show ip interface brief': columns are Interface, IP-Address, OK?, Method, Status, and Protocol ]
Example output of 'show ip interface brief': columns are Interface, IP-Address, OK?, Method, Status, and Protocol
Status column (Layer 1): 'up' means cable connected and physical signal detected. 'administratively down' means manually disabled with the 'shutdown' command.
Protocol column (Layer 2): 'up' means data link layer is functioning. 'down' means Layer 2 has failed even if Layer 1 is up.
Important: Router interfaces are administratively down by default — must be manually enabled with 'no shutdown'. Switch interfaces come up automatically when a device is physically connected.
Cisco IOS — Configuration Files:-
Running-Config (stored in RAM — volatile): the active configuration currently running on the device. Every CLI command immediately modifies this file. Lost completely on reboot without saving.
Startup-Config (stored in Non-Volatile RAM (NVRAM) — non-volatile): the configuration that loads on boot. Must be explicitly updated by saving the running configuration.
show running-config                    → view the current active configuration
show startup-config                    → view the saved startup configuration
copy running-config startup-config     → save running config to NVRAM (persists across reboots)
write memory                           → alternative shorthand for the above
Tip: Always save your configuration before rebooting. Unsaved changes in RAM are permanently lost when the device restarts.
Dynamic Routing Protocols

Static routes require manual configuration and do not adapt to network changes. Dynamic routing protocols allow routers to automatically discover networks, share route information with neighbors, and update their routing tables when the topology changes.
Dynamic Routing Fundamentals:-

Routers running a dynamic routing protocol form adjacencies (also called neighbor relationships or neighborships) with directly connected routers and exchange routing information automatically. When multiple routes to the same destination are learned, the router selects the best one using the route's metric — a value that represents the cost of using that path. A lower metric is always preferred.
Network route: a route to a network or subnet (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24).
Host route: a route to a single specific host, using a /32 prefix (e.g., 192.168.1.1/32).
Administrative Distance (AD):-

When a router learns routes from multiple different routing protocols, it needs a way to decide which protocol's routes to trust. Administrative Distance (AD) is a value assigned to each routing source that indicates its trustworthiness. A lower AD is more preferred.

rows: EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) Summary Route
255 — route is never installed in the routing table

blocks.text: Note: Metric is used to compare routes learned via the same routing protocol. Administrative Distance (AD) is used to compare routes learned via different routing protocols. You cannot compare metrics across different protocols.
Floating Static Routes:-
The Administrative Distance of a static route can be manually increased so that it is only used when a dynamic routing protocol's route to the same destination is no longer available:
ip route <network> <mask> <next-hop> <AD>     → configure a static route with a custom AD
This is called a floating static route. It sits in the background and becomes active only if the dynamic route disappears — for example, when a neighbor adjacency is lost or an interface fails.
Equal Cost Multi-Path (ECMP):-

If a router learns two or more routes to the same destination via the same routing protocol with the same metric, all routes are added to the routing table and traffic is load-balanced across them. This is called Equal Cost Multi-Path (ECMP). Most routing protocols support up to 4 ECMP paths by default.
Routing Protocol Categories:-

rows: Used to share routes within a single Autonomous System (AS) — typically one organization.
Used to share routes between different Autonomous Systems — between organizations or ISPs.
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) — the only EGP in use today

blocks.text: Distance Vector Protocols:-

Distance Vector protocols share route information by sending their known destinations and metrics to directly connected neighbors only. Each router knows the direction (next hop) and distance (metric) to reach a destination, but has no knowledge of the full network topology beyond its neighbors. This is often called 'routing by rumor'. Examples: Routing Information Protocol (RIP), Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP).
Link State Protocols:-

Link State protocols work differently — each router advertises information about its own directly connected interfaces to all routers in the network. These advertisements (called Link State Advertisements (LSAs)) are flooded through the entire area until every router has an identical map of the network. Each router then independently runs the Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm on this map to calculate the best routes. Link State protocols react faster to network changes than Distance Vector protocols, but use more CPU and memory resources. Examples: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF), Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS).
Routing Information Protocol (RIP):-

Routing Information Protocol (RIP) is a Distance Vector Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP). It uses hop count as its metric — each router in the path counts as one hop, regardless of bandwidth. The maximum hop count is 15; any destination more than 15 hops away is considered unreachable.
RIP-enabled routers share their full routing table with neighbors every 30 seconds using two message types:
Request: asks a RIP-enabled neighbor to send its routing table.
Response: sends the local router's routing table to neighbors.
Configuring RIP:-
router rip                          → enter RIP configuration mode
version 2                           → use RIPv2 (recommended)
no auto-summary                     → disable automatic classful summarization (on by default — must be disabled for VLSM/CIDR support)
network <network-address>           → activate RIP on interfaces matching this classful network range

The 'network' command is classful — it automatically converts the address to its classful boundary. For example, 'network 10.0.12.0' becomes 'network 10.0.0.0' (Class A). The network command does not tell RIP which networks to advertise. It tells RIP which interfaces to activate on, and the router then advertises the actual prefix of each activated interface.
passive-interface g#/#             → stop sending RIP advertisements out of this interface (still advertises the prefix to neighbors)

Always configure passive-interface on interfaces that have no RIP neighbors — such as interfaces connected to end hosts. This prevents unnecessary RIP traffic and avoids exposing routing information to end devices. EIGRP and OSPF use the same passive-interface command.
default-information originate      → advertise a default route (0.0.0.0/0) to RIP neighbors
show ip protocols                  → view active routing protocol configuration and settings
Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP):-

Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) was originally Cisco-proprietary but has since been published as an open standard. It is considered an advanced or hybrid Distance Vector protocol. EIGRP reacts to topology changes much faster than RIP and has no hop-count limit. It uses multicast address 224.0.0.10 to communicate with neighbors. By default it performs Equal Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) over up to 4 paths — and uniquely, it is the only Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) that can also perform unequal-cost load balancing.
Configuring EIGRP:-
router eigrp <AS-number>            → enter EIGRP configuration mode. The Autonomous System (AS) number must match on all routers — mismatched AS numbers prevent adjacency formation.
no auto-summary                     → disable classful summarization
network <ip-address> <wildcard-mask> → activate EIGRP on interfaces matching this range

EIGRP uses a wildcard mask — the inverse of a subnet mask. A 0 bit in the wildcard mask means 'this bit must match'; a 1 bit means 'this bit can be anything'. Example: subnet mask 255.255.255.0 = wildcard mask 0.0.0.255.
eigrp router-id <#.#.#.#>          → manually set the EIGRP Router ID
show ip eigrp neighbors            → view established EIGRP neighbor adjacencies
show ip eigrp topology            → view the EIGRP topology table (all learned routes, not just best routes)
EIGRP Metric:-

By default, EIGRP calculates its metric using bandwidth and delay: metric = bandwidth of the slowest link + cumulative delay of all links. The simplified formula is: Metric = (Bandwidth + Delay) × 256.
Feasible Distance (FD): this router's total metric to the destination.
Reported Distance (RD) / Advertised Distance (AD): the neighbor's metric to the destination (as reported to this router).
Successor: the route with the lowest Feasible Distance — the best route, installed in the routing table.

Feasible Successor: an alternate route whose Reported Distance is lower than the Successor's Feasible Distance. Meets the feasibility condition — a loop prevention mechanism. Feasible Successors are stored in the topology table as instant backups.
EIGRP Unequal-Cost Load Balancing (Variance):-

EIGRP can load-balance across routes with different metrics using the variance multiplier. Variance 1 (default) = only ECMP. Variance 2 = feasible successor routes with a Feasible Distance up to 2× the successor's Feasible Distance can participate in load balancing. EIGRP will only use Feasible Successors for unequal-cost load balancing — a route that does not meet the feasibility condition can never be used, regardless of variance.
Router ID Priority Order (EIGRP and OSPF):-
Manually configured Router ID.
Highest IP address on a loopback interface.
Highest IP address on a physical interface.
To create a loopback interface and assign an IP address:
int loopback <number>
ip address <ip-address> <subnet-mask>
Open Shortest Path First (OSPF):-

Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) is a Link State Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP). It uses Dijkstra's Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm to calculate the best routes. OSPF routers store network topology information in Link State Advertisements (LSAs), which are organized in a Link State Database (LSDB). All routers in an OSPF area flood LSAs until every router has an identical LSDB, then each independently calculates the best routes.

rows: Used for IPv4. The standard version in use today.
Used for IPv6. Can also support IPv4 but OSPFv2 is typically used for IPv4.

blocks.text: OSPF Areas:-

OSPF divides the network into areas to improve scalability. In a large single-area OSPF network, every topology change causes all routers to re-run the SPF algorithm and reflood LSAs — consuming CPU, memory, and bandwidth. Dividing the network into multiple areas limits the scope of these updates.
Area 0 (Backbone Area): the central area that all other areas must connect to directly.
Internal Router: all interfaces are in the same OSPF area.
Area Border Router (ABR): has interfaces in multiple areas. Maintains a separate LSDB for each area. Recommended maximum of 2 areas per ABR — connecting to 3 or more areas can overburden the router.
Backbone Router: any router with an interface in Area 0.
Autonomous System Boundary Router (ASBR): an OSPF router that connects the OSPF network to an external network (e.g., the internet). Using 'default-information originate' makes a router an ASBR.
Intra-area route: a route to a destination within the same OSPF area.
Inter-area route: a route to a destination in a different OSPF area.
Note: All OSPF areas must be contiguous (connected). All areas must connect to the backbone area (Area 0). OSPF interfaces in the same subnet must be in the same area.
Configuring OSPF:-
router ospf <process-id>            → enter OSPF configuration mode. The process ID is locally significant — routers with different process IDs can still become neighbors.
network <ip-address> <wildcard-mask> area <area-id>  → activate OSPF on interfaces matching this range and assign them to the specified area
Alternatively, OSPF can be activated directly on an interface:
int <interface-id>
ip ospf <process-id> area <area-id> → activate OSPF on this interface directly (replaces the network command)
router-id <#.#.#.#>                → manually configure the OSPF Router ID (same priority order as EIGRP)
passive-interface <interface-id>   → stop sending OSPF Hello messages out of this interface (still advertises the subnet in LSAs)
passive-interface default          → make ALL interfaces passive by default
no passive-interface <interface-id> → re-activate a specific interface after using passive-interface default
default-information originate      → advertise a default route into OSPF (makes this router an ASBR)
maximum-paths <number>             → change the maximum number of ECMP paths (default is 4)
OSPF Metric — Cost:-
OSPF's metric is called cost. It is calculated by dividing the reference bandwidth by the interface bandwidth. The default reference bandwidth is 100 Mbps:

Because any value below 1 is rounded up to 1, FastEthernet, Gigabit, and 10 Gigabit all have the same default cost of 1 — which makes them indistinguishable to OSPF. To fix this, change the reference bandwidth to a value greater than your fastest link:
auto-cost reference-bandwidth <Mbps>  → change the reference bandwidth (configure the same value on ALL OSPF routers)
Three ways to set the OSPF cost on an interface (highest priority first):
Direct cost override:  ip ospf cost <value>  — takes priority over all other methods.
Change interface bandwidth:  bandwidth <Kbps>  — affects cost calculation but also affects EIGRP metric. Not recommended.
Change the reference bandwidth:  auto-cost reference-bandwidth  — affects all interfaces globally.
The total OSPF cost to a destination is the sum of the costs of all outgoing (exit) interfaces along the path — the same concept as STP path cost. Loopback interfaces always have a cost of 1.
OSPF DR and BDR:-

On broadcast network types (Ethernet by default), OSPF elects a Designated Router (DR) and a Backup Designated Router (BDR) on each subnet to reduce the number of LSA exchanges. Without a DR/BDR, every pair of routers on the segment would need to form a full adjacency — creating n(n-1)/2 adjacencies for n routers.
DR: all routers on the segment form a Full adjacency with the DR and exchange LSAs through it.
BDR: monitors the DR and takes over if the DR fails.
DROther: any router that is not the DR or BDR. DROthers form a Full adjacency only with the DR and BDR — they remain in the 2-Way state with other DROthers.
DR/BDR election priority order:
Highest OSPF interface priority (default is 1 on all interfaces — set to 0 to prevent a router from being elected DR/BDR).
Highest OSPF Router ID.
'First place' becomes the DR; 'second place' becomes the BDR. The election is non-preemptive — once elected, the DR and BDR keep their roles until OSPF is reset or the interface fails.
ip ospf priority <0-255>            → change the OSPF priority on an interface (0 = never DR/BDR)
When the DR goes down, the BDR immediately becomes the new DR, and a new BDR election is held among the remaining DROthers.
OSPF Neighbor States:-
OSPF routers go through a series of states before establishing a full adjacency and exchanging their LSDBs:

rows: OSPF activated on the interface. Hello messages sent to 224.0.0.5. No neighbors known yet.
A Hello packet was received from a neighbor, but this router's own Router ID is not yet in the neighbor's Hello packet.

Both routers have seen each other's Router ID in Hello packets. All conditions for adjacency are met. On broadcast networks, the DR/BDR election occurs here. DROthers remain in the 2-Way state with each other.
The routers negotiate which will be Master (higher Router ID) and which will be Slave before exchanging Database Description (DBD) packets.
Routers exchange Database Description (DBD) packets — summaries of their LSDBs — to find out what LSAs the other router has.
Routers send Link State Request (LSR) messages to request specific LSAs they are missing. LSAs are delivered in Link State Update (LSU) messages and acknowledged with LSAck messages.
Routers have identical LSDBs and a complete OSPF adjacency. They continue exchanging Hello packets to maintain the adjacency (Hello every 10 s, Dead timer 40 s).

blocks.text: Note: OSPF Hello messages are multicast to 224.0.0.5 (all OSPF routers). Messages to the Designated Router (DR) and Backup Designated Router (BDR) use 224.0.0.6. OSPF is encapsulated directly in IP with Protocol field value 89.
OSPF Network Types:-

rows: Default for Ethernet. DR/BDR reduce LSA flooding.
Only 2 routers — no need for DR/BDR. Routers go directly to Full state.
Manually configure neighbors. DR/BDR elected but no multicast.

blocks.text: On serial interfaces, one side functions as DCE (Data Communications Equipment) and the other as DTE (Data Terminal Equipment). The DCE side must set the clock rate (speed):
clock rate <bits-per-second>        → set the clock rate on the DCE side of a serial link
show controllers <interface-id>    → identify which side is DCE and which is DTE
The default encapsulation on serial interfaces is Cisco HDLC (cHDLC). To change it (must match on both ends):
encapsulation <ppp|hdlc>            → change the serial encapsulation
To change the OSPF network type on an interface:
ip ospf network <broadcast|point-to-point|non-broadcast>   → override the default network type
OSPF Timers and Authentication:-
ip ospf hello-interval <seconds>   → change the Hello timer (default 10 s on Ethernet)
